digest.definition: Education Studies studies how people develop and learn across their lives, the nature of knowledge and ways of knowing and educational processes and systems in their cultural, social, technological, political, philosophical, environmental, historical and economic settings, always with critique of policy and practice
distinctiveFeatures: Education Studies studies how people develop and learn across their lives, the nature of knowledge and ways of knowing and educational processes and systems in their cultural, social, technological, political, philosophical, environmental, historical and economic settings, always with critique of policy and practice
It joins theory and scholarly practice (praxis) and aims to change lives and society for the better, preparing students to act as agents of change
It can be read as a subject defined by content, a field drawing on psychology, sociology, philosophy, history, language, politics and economics, or a discipline with its own discourses and methods
Ethics runs through all of it, and it is always changing
Learning is reciprocal: students bring diverse perspectives that feed critical debate
It treats education in its widest sense, well beyond schools, colleges and universities, and its graduates go into many sectors, not only teaching
Its curriculum spans three overlapping areas, subject-specific, practice-based and transversal, where transformative learning happens at their meeting point

statements.appliesTo: students of Education Studies
statements.about: taking a reasoned position in educational debate
statements.paraphrase: Students take part in, build and challenge debates about values, engagement, educational practice and community; by choosing, analysing and combining viewpoints they grow critical capability and so can hold a reasoned stance in a world that keeps changing, ready for many careers and for learning across working life.

forPractitioner.text: Give students room to join, shape and contest debates on values and practice, and to choose, analyse and combine viewpoints until they can hold and defend a reasoned stance; tie this to their future careers and continued learning.

forBeneficiary.text: You can take part in, shape and question debates about values, practice and communities, and you learn to choose, analyse and combine viewpoints so that you can argue for a reasoned stance of your own.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Education Studies degree

statements.appliesTo: students of Education Studies
statements.about: questioning entrenched language, knowledge and thought
statements.paraphrase: Students can question core concepts and terms, recognising how dominant ways of speaking, knowing and thinking have become fixed, in the past and now, across formal, informal and hidden curricula.

forPractitioner.text: Build in tasks where students question the key terms and concepts of education and trace how dominant language and knowledge have taken hold in formal, informal and hidden curricula.

forBeneficiary.text: You can question the key ideas and terms you meet, and see how dominant ways of speaking, knowing and thinking have taken hold in what is taught openly, informally and in the hidden curriculum.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Education Studies degree

statements.appliesTo: students of Education Studies
statements.about: engaging with EDI and taking a position on justice
statements.paraphrase: Students can work with questions of equity, diversity and inclusion, seeing what helping to build a just society involves, recognising differing standpoints and setting out where they stand, both in terms of rights, duties, responsibilities and law and beyond them.

forPractitioner.text: Ask students to work through EDI questions, weigh different standpoints and state their own position with reference to rights, duties, responsibilities and the law, and also beyond those frames.

forBeneficiary.text: You can work with questions of equity, diversity and inclusion, see what it takes to help build a fairer society, recognise other people's standpoints and say clearly where you stand.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Education Studies degree

statements.appliesTo: Education Studies courses and their students
statements.about: reflection, self-understanding and respect for divergent views
statements.paraphrase: Courses give students the agency to reflect, question and take part; students are practised in reflection and can see what is distinctive about themselves while showing proper respect for views that differ from or oppose their own.

forPractitioner.text: Give students real scope to reflect, question and take part, and assess reflection that pairs self-understanding with respect for views far from their own.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course gives you room to reflect, question and take part, and you can become skilled at reflection, understanding what is distinctive about you while respecting views that differ sharply from yours.

statements.appliesTo: Education Studies courses and their teams
statements.about: the Equality Act duty to anticipate accessibility issues
statements.paraphrase: The Equality Act 2010 puts a legal duty on education providers to act ahead of need rather than after it, foreseeing accessibility issues in teaching, learning and assessment.

forPractitioner.text: Treat accessibility in teaching, learning and assessment as something to plan for in advance, as the Equality Act 2010 requires of the institution, not something to fix once a problem appears.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or the institution, not a standard the student reaches

statements.appliesTo: Education Studies courses and their teams
statements.about: accessibility in course design and the wider student experience
statements.paraphrase: The subject is inclusive and open to everyone, including students from varied social and economic backgrounds, with specific learning needs, neurodivergent students and those who need particular access arrangements; it treats accessibility as both a moral and a legal imperative that must be considered in course design and in planning the wider student experience.

forPractitioner.text: Build accessibility into the course design itself and into planning the wider student experience, for students with specific learning needs, access requirements or neurodivergence and from every background: this is a must, not an option.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or the institution, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Course curriculum, content and assessment need to be open to every learner, whatever their culture, disability, neurodivergence, identity or background, and every assessment should be clear about its purpose and what it expects.

forPractitioner.text: Check curriculum, content and assessment for access across cultures, disabilities, neurodivergence, identities and backgrounds, and make each assessment brief state its purpose and expectations clearly.

statements.paraphrase: Students understand the distinctive and vital part education plays in a sustainable future, through learning across life and in many formal and informal settings; although some parts of a course may treat these themes on their own, course teams should consider teaching, content and assessment in a broader frame.

forPractitioner.text: Spread sustainability across teaching, content and assessment rather than leaving it to one module, and help students see how learning across life and settings serves a sustainable future.

forBeneficiary.text: You will come to understand the part education plays in a sustainable future, through learning at every age and in many settings, and your course should weave sustainability through its teaching, content and assessment.

statements.about: progression through the levels to the threshold
statements.paraphrase: Students on an honours degree (FHEQ Level 6; FQHEIS Level 10) or, where offered, an integrated master's (FHEQ Level 7; FQHEIS Level 11) will move through the levels under each institution's rules, each level adding knowledge, expertise and experience towards meeting the threshold skills of the statement (and any higher ones set); this will usually mean passing, and gaining credit for, all learning and assessment, practical parts included.

forBeneficiary.text: You will move from one level of study to the next, each one building your knowledge, expertise and experience towards the standards for your degree, and you will usually need to pass every part, practical work included.
